content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a gasoline-powered mower for an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. Users can manually drive the robot along the lawn boundary to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe this machine may be easier for many people to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each robot understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I needed to manually drive the mower along the boundary with an iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map the lawn, with no need to bury boundary wires or install a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less tech-savvy.

To verify this claim, I asked my mother, who lives in another state, to install and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She said everything worked fine. That said, I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire boundary with her phone, and then mark out all the areas that need to be avoided.

The automatic mapping caused a small issue in my front yard. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn within my map area.

I marked that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the issue was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, you need to be extra careful when building the initial map.

Peeking through the mower's camera

The camera on the TerraMow also brings one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used iPhone screen mirroring on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could sit inside working while watching from the mower's perspective as it navigated the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and can sometimes explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps have quite a lot in common. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone division, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has a particularly nice variation on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule without any intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is quite fun for cleaning up small patches that the robot missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I am controlling the robot by telekinesis (the fun kind). I walk beside the mower holding my iPhone, barely moving my thumb, and the robot follows my instructions.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder in operation.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow 'noisy,' but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly—so quietly it's easy to forget it's still going, including when it mows at night using its headlight.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage covering the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for daily mowing for several weeks without needing to intervene.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you can't perform other actions in the app.

After several days of continuous rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. A puddle appeared somewhere in the yard, and the TerraMow reasonably avoided that area on its next run.

Within the skipped circular area, the weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret the growth there as an object that needed to be continually avoided, and even after the ground dried out, that area was still always skipped.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower over to trim the taller grass there, and the issue was resolved. Once the area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging can also help the TerraMow reach the boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing on faint boundary lines might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. That method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids the map 'changing its mind' about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac conclusion

Having used both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying boundary wires is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means having to place, power, and maintain extra hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, invisible property boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook an overgrown patch for a permanent obstacle.

These issues remain manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, compelling live camera views, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I have used.

I do enjoy looking after the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this job over to a robot frees up my time for garden arrangement, edging, and detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels at this, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but don't want to bury boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard with their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, the price after applying a US$200 coupon on the site. The product is also available on TerraMow's official website.
